full_text:
In a grand kingdom nestled between rolling green hills and misty pine forests, a noble king and queen long wept for lack of a child. When at last a daughter was born to them, their joy was beyond measure, and they proclaimed a magnificent christening feast that echoed through the marble courtyards of the palace. To bless the royal infant, they invited seven ancient and benevolent fairies who dwelt in the hidden grottos of the realm, bestowing upon each an ornate case of pure gold containing a spoon, knife, and fork wrought of heavy silver and studded with diamonds and rubies.

As the guests took their seats at the banquet table, the great carved oak doors groaned open. An eighth fairy, an elderly crone who had not emerged from her mossy tower in fifty years and was believed by the entire court to be dead or enchanted, hobbled into the hall on an ebony staff. The king hastily bade her welcome, but because only seven golden cases had been crafted, she was given service in fine porcelain and silver. Slighting herself insulted, the old fairy muttered dark venom under her breath as she took her seat.

When the feast ended, the fairies approached the cradle of cedar and silk to bestow their supernatural gifts. The first fairy gave the princess beauty surpassing the petals of the morning rose; the second gave her the spirit and wit of an angel; the third gave her grace in every movement; the fourth gave her the voice of a celestial nightingale; the fifth gave her skill upon the harp and lute; and the sixth gifted her nimble lightness in dance.

Then the vengeful old fairy stepped forward, shaking with spite. Leaning over the cradle, she hissed: 'My gift is this: when the princess is in her sixteenth summer, she shall prick her hand upon the spindle of a spinning wheel, and she shall instantly die!' A chill seized the hall; the queen fainted into the arms of her ladies, and the courtiers wept in despair.

At that moment, a young fairy who had prudently hidden behind the velvet tapestries stepped forth. 'Grieve not, Your Majesties,' she said in a soothing voice like running water. 'My magic cannot wholly overturn the ancient curse, but it can soften its sting. The princess shall not die. When the spindle pricks her tender finger, she shall fall into a deep, peaceful slumber lasting one hundred years, until a king's son arrives to awaken her.'

Desperate to shield his beloved child, the king issued a stern royal decree forbidding any soul in the realm to spin with a spindle or keep a spinning wheel in their dwelling under penalty of death. For fifteen years, the princess grew into radiant grace, beloved by all who beheld her. On the day of her sixteenth birthday, while exploring the upper turrets of a secluded forest chateau, she climbed a winding stone stair and came upon an attic chamber where an honest old peasant woman sat alone, whirring her distaff, having never heard of the king's distant proclamation.

'What are you doing, grandmother?' the girl asked with childlike curiosity. 'May I try the spinning rod?' As she reached out her hand, the whirling wooden needle pricked her fingertip. In an instant, her breath slowed, her eyes closed in peaceful rest, and she sank onto a bed embroidered with gold, asleep in perfect stillness.

The good fairy who had softened the curse arrived in a chariot of fire drawn by winged dragons. Knowing the princess would be terrified to wake alone in a distant century, she touched with her wand every creature in the castle—the royal guards, the lord chamberlain, the maids of honor, the cooks in the kitchen, the spit-turning turnspit dog, and the stallions in the marble stables. All fell into enchanted slumber. Outside, great brambles, dense hawthorns, and towering oaks sprang from the earth, weaving an impassable thicket that concealed the castle towers from mortal sight.

A century passed like a single night. A brave prince from a neighboring dynasty was hunting deer when he saw the ancient stone spires rising above the mysterious forest. An elderly peasant recounted the old legend: that a sleeping princess of unmatched beauty lay within, awaiting the destined royal touch. With courage in his heart, the prince pushed toward the briars; to his wonder, the thorny branches parted like silk curtains, allowing him to pass.

He strode through silent courtyards where guards slept leaning on their halberds and dogs rested with their paws across their noses. Reaching the high gilded chamber, he beheld the princess, whose cheeks still bloomed with the freshness of youth. Overcome with reverence and love, he knelt beside her couch and gently took her warm hand.

Her eyelids fluttered open, her sapphire eyes met his, and she whispered: 'Is it you, my prince? You have kept me waiting long.' At that instant, the spell broke. Roosters crowed, the kitchen spits resumed their turning, the guards saluted, and the chapel bells chimed. Joined in marriage before the assembled court, the prince and princess governed with wisdom and compassion, proving that no darkness of malice can ever extinguish the light of destined hope.
moral: Patience and virtue endure through the longest trials, and true goodness awakens beauty in its appointed time.

full_text:
Once upon a time, at the sunny edge of a vast and ancient forest, there lived a cheerful, sweet-tempered village girl who was adored by everyone who met her, but most of all by her doting grandmother. The elderly woman had sewn for the girl a handsome cloak and hood of scarlet velvet that suited her so wonderfully that the villagers and travelers called her by no other name than Little Red Riding Hood.

One bright morning, her mother took a batch of golden, freshly baked honey cakes from the clay oven and sealed a crock of sweet country butter with a clean linen cloth. 'Come, Little Red Riding Hood,' her mother said, adjusting the girl's crimson cape. 'Your grandmother has taken a fever and lies weak in her cottage on the other side of the woods. Carry these cakes and butter to her to restore her strength. Walk briskly and politely; do not stray from the worn stone path into the thickets, and speak to no strangers along the way.'

The girl kissed her mother's cheek and promised to obey every word. Skipping down the trail with her woven willow basket on her arm, she entered the dappled shade of the great pine forest. The woodland was alive with the singing of thrushes and the scent of wild strawberries, and the girl soon forgot the urgency of her errand.

Deep in the pines, a gray wolf of enormous size and cunning mind caught the scent of the sweet butter and the tender traveler. He longed to seize her upon the spot, but the ringing thuds of woodcutters' iron axes echoed through the trees nearby, and he dared not attack openly. Stepping softly from behind a mossy boulder, the wolf bowed low with feigned courtly manners.

'Good day, fair maiden,' the wolf murmured in his smoothest, gentlest voice. 'Whither are you hastening so early with such a delightful basket?'

Remembering nothing of her mother's warning because the wolf seemed so polite, the girl replied: 'I am carrying fresh honey cakes and butter to my grandmother, who is bedridden with illness.'

'And where does your dear grandmother live?' inquired the sly beast, licking his whiskers.

'Past the old flour mill, in the first cottage of the adjoining village, sheltered under the three great oak trees,' she answered cheerfully.

'A noble duty!' said the wolf, his yellow eyes gleaming. 'See how the forest blooms with bluebells and wild violets. Why not gather a fragrant bouquet to brighten her sickbed while I stroll ahead to announce your coming?'

While the unsuspecting girl wandered deep into the leafy undergrowth picking blossoms, the wolf ran with all his might along the straight shortcut. Reaching the cottage under the three oaks, he tapped lightly on the wooden door: tap, tap.

'Who is there?' called the weak voice of the grandmother from her feather bed.

'It is your grandchild, Little Red Riding Hood,' the wolf whispered, pitching his voice high. 'I bring you warm cakes and butter from mother.'

The trusting woman called out: 'Pull the bobbin, my child, and the latch will go up.'

The wolf pulled the bobbin, burst into the bedchamber, and leaped upon the bed, swallowing the poor grandmother whole before she could utter a cry. Then, donning her lace nightcap and bedgown, he drew the heavy floral curtains of the four-poster bed and hid beneath the quilts, chuckling at his evil triumph.

Presently, Little Red Riding Hood arrived with an apron full of wild flowers. Tapping on the door, she heard a gruff, raspy voice call out: 'Who is there?' Startled for a moment, the girl thought her grandmother's throat must be terribly hoarse from the fever. She answered sweetly, pulled the bobbin, and entered the quiet cottage.

Approaching the shaded bed, the girl felt an uneasy shiver. 'Grandmother,' she said softly, 'what great big ears you have!'

'The better to hear you with, my child,' the wolf replied from beneath the lace cap.

'Grandmother, what great big eyes you have!'

'The better to see you with, my darling.'

'Grandmother, what enormous hands you have!'

'The better to embrace you with, my sweet.'

'And grandmother... what dreadful, gigantic teeth you have!'

'The better to EAT YOU WITH!' howled the wolf, throwing back the covers and springing into the air.

Just as the beast snapped his jaws, the heavy wooden door was kicked wide. A stalwart woodsman, who had noticed the wolf's pawprints turning toward the secluded cottage, burst into the room brandishing his polished iron felling axe. With a single, mighty blow, the woodsman struck down the ravenous predator. With his hunting knife, he slit open the belly of the beast, and out stepped the grandmother and Little Red Riding Hood, shaken but completely unharmed!

They filled the wolf's coat with heavy river stones and drove him into the wild gorge, never to threaten the forest again. Together, the three sat by the warm hearth to share the honey cakes and sweet butter. Little Red Riding Hood hugged her grandmother tightly and vowed never again to stray from the path or trust the flattering words of strangers.
moral: Children must heed the counsel of their parents, beware of smooth-talking strangers, and keep securely to the safe path.

title: La Barbe bleue - Blue Beard
summary: There lived once a nobleman of immense wealth, possessing splendid townhouses with marble terraces, carriages lined with gilded velvet, a...
full_text:
There lived once a nobleman of immense wealth, possessing splendid townhouses with marble terraces, carriages lined with gilded velvet, and services of solid gold and silver. Yet this lord was universally feared and shunned throughout the province because his beard was of an uncanny, midnight-blue hue, so grotesque that women and children trembled whenever he rode past.

Seeking a wife, Bluebeard paid court to the two fair daughters of a noble neighbor. Both maidens shrank from his suit, not only because of his dreadful beard, but because several wives had married him in years past, and not a single soul knew what had become of them. To soften their dread, Bluebeard invited the mother, daughters, and their friends to his opulent country chateau for an entire week of feasts, dances, hunting parties, and fireworks.

The entertainment was so enchanting that the younger daughter began to think his beard was not so blue after all, and that he was a most courteous gentleman. Soon after their return, the marriage was celebrated with great pomp.

A month later, Bluebeard informed his young wife that pressing affairs of state required him to journey to the distant provinces for six weeks. Handing her a massive iron ring carrying the keys to all his treasures, he said: 'Here are the keys to the grand wardrobes, the jewel vaults, the iron strongboxes of bullion, and the master keys that unlock every apartment in the palace. Make merry with your friends, spare no expense, and feast on whatever pleases your heart. But observe this small key of polished gold: it opens the low closet at the end of the long stone gallery on the ground floor. Open any chamber you wish, but I strictly forbid you to enter that closet. If you turn this key in its lock, expect my unyielding wrath.'

The young bride promised faithfully to respect his commandment, kissed him goodbye, and watched his carriage depart. Her companions flocked to the chateau, marveling at the silk tapestries, Venetian mirrors, and crystal chandeliers. Yet amidst their laughter, the bride could think of nothing but the forbidden closet. Driven by irresistible curiosity, she left her guests and hurried down the winding private stairs.

Reaching the secluded doorway, her hands trembled. She paused, remembering her husband's grave warning, but the burning desire to know conquered all prudence. She inserted the little golden key and turned the lock. The heavy door swung inward.

The chamber was dark and cold. As her eyes adjusted, she gasped in horror: the floor was strewn with dark stains, and within the shadowed alcoves lay the remains of Bluebeard's former wives, whom he had murdered for their curiosity. Paralyzed with terror, she dropped the golden key upon the flagstones. Picking it up with shaking fingers, she locked the door and fled to her private bedchamber.

Looking at the key, she noticed a stain of blood upon its polished tooth. She washed it with well water; she scrubbed it with scented soap; she rubbed it with pumice stone and emery powder. But the key was enchanted by dark sorcery: when the stain was cleansed from one side, it reappeared upon the other.

That very evening, Bluebeard returned unexpectedly, explaining that messengers had brought news settling his business favorably. He received his trembling wife with polite smiles, asking for his bunch of keys on the following morning. She surrendered them with pale cheeks, but the little golden key was missing.

'Where is the key to the closet at the gallery's end?' Bluebeard demanded, his brow darkening like thunder.

'I must have left it upon my dressing table, my lord,' she stammered.

'Bring it to me immediately,' he commanded.

When she placed the key in his palm, Bluebeard saw the crimson stain and sneered: 'How came this blood upon the metal? You entered the forbidden chamber, madam! Since you were so eager to see what lay within, you shall take your permanent place beside the ladies who came before you.'

The weeping bride fell at his feet, pleading for mercy with heartfelt tears. 'You must die,' Bluebeard roared, drawing his heavy steel scimitar.

'Grant me but seven minutes to say my prayers and commend my soul to heaven,' she begged.

'You have seven minutes,' growled the tyrant, 'and not a breath longer.'

Left alone, the young wife ran to the high stone turret where her sister Anne was watching the countryside. 'Anne, sister Anne!' she cried. 'Look out into the road and tell me if our two brothers are coming! They promised to visit us this morning!'

Sister Anne peered into the morning haze: 'I see only the sun making dust dance and the green grass growing.'

Below, Bluebeard shouted with a voice that shook the walls: 'Come down, madam, or I shall fetch you!'

'One moment more!' she begged, calling upward: 'Anne, sister Anne, do you see nothing coming?'

'I see a cloud of dust rising toward the east!' Anne called down. 'Alas, it is but a flock of sheep driven by a shepherd.'

'Your time has expired!' bellowed Bluebeard, his boots thundering up the stone stairs. He seized his wife by her golden hair, raising his blade to strike off her head.

At that desperate instant, the courtyard gates were battered down with a thunderous crash. Two mounted cavaliers—one a royal dragoon and the other a musketeer—dashed into the courtyard with drawn swords. Recognizing the bride's brothers, Bluebeard turned to flee, but the brave brothers pursued him across the terrace and ran him through with their blades, ending his reign of terror forever.

The young widow inherited the vast estates of Bluebeard. She provided an honorable dowry for sister Anne, purchased captaincies in the royal guard for her valiant brothers, and eventually married an honorable, noble gentleman whose kindness healed the memory of her ordeal, living out her days in peace, generosity, and joy.
moral: Curiosity indulged against wise counsel brings peril, but truth, courage, and family loyalty triumph over tyranny.

full_text:
An honest miller died, leaving behind nothing in this world to his three sons except his watermill, his donkey, and his tomcat. The division of property was swift: the eldest son took the mill, the second took the donkey, while the youngest was left with only the cat.

The poor young man sat on a milestone, wringing his hands in despair. 'My brothers can join their trades together and earn an honest living,' he lamented, 'but as for me, when I have cooked this cat and made a fur muff of his skin, I must die of starvation on the highway.'

The cat, who was washing his whiskers in the grass, heard every word. Sitting upright on his hind paws, he looked at his master with shrewd, luminous eyes and said: 'Do not grieve, my good master. Only provide me with a sturdy canvas sack with running cords, and have a shoemaker craft me a pair of polished leather boots so that I may walk without slipping through brambles and briars, and you shall soon discover that your inheritance is far more valuable than you imagine.'

Though astonished to hear a cat speak, the miller's son remembered how cleverly the feline had hunted rats by feigning death in the flour bins. With his last few silver coins, he purchased the leather boots and the bag.

Puss buckled the boots onto his paws, slung the corded bag across his shoulders, and trotted into a nearby warren where young, plump wild rabbits fed upon fresh clover. He filled the sack with bran and tender parsley, laid the bag open on the ground, and stretched himself out like a dead carcass, holding the cords between his claws. Presently, a foolish young rabbit hopped into the sack to feast. Puss pulled the strings tight, bagged the prize, and set off with pride for the royal palace.

Arriving at the throne room, Puss bowed to the ground before the King. 'Sire,' he purred with courtly elegance, 'I present you with this wild rabbit from the estates of my noble master, the Marquis of Carabas, who has commanded me to lay this humble gift at your feet.'

'Tell your master,' the King replied, pleased by the fine game, 'that I thank him heartily and receive his gift with pleasure.'

A few days later, Puss concealed himself in a wheat field with his open sack and captured two plump partridges. He carried them to the King as a gift from the Marquis of Carabas, receiving another purse of silver and royal gratitude. For three months, the booted cat regularly carried gifts of game to the court, making the name of the Marquis of Carabas renowned for wealth and generosity.

One day, Puss learned that the King was to ride in his golden carriage along the banks of the river with his daughter, the most beautiful princess in the world. Rushing to his master, Puss ordered: 'Strip off your ragged clothes and jump into the river to bathe where I direct you, and leave the rest of your fortune in my paws!'

The miller's son obeyed without question. As the royal carriage approached, Puss leaped onto the road, wailing at the top of his lungs: 'Help! Help! The Marquis of Carabas is drowning! Save my lord!'

The King put his head out of the carriage window and recognized the booted cat who had brought him so many partridges. He immediately ordered his royal guards to plunge into the river and rescue the young man. While the drenched youth was pulled to safety, Puss approached the King and whispered that while his master was swimming, rogue thieves had stolen his magnificent garments (having concealed the old clothes under a large flat rock).

The King instantly commanded the grand master of the wardrobe to bring one of his own finest embroidered suits of velvet and satin. Dressed in royal attire, the miller's son appeared so handsome, tall, and noble that the princess fell deeply in love with him at first sight, and the King invited him to ride inside the royal coach.

Overjoyed, Puss ran ahead along the road. Coming upon peasants mowing grass in a lush meadow, he hissed fiercely: 'Good people! If you do not tell the King when he passes that this meadow belongs to the Marquis of Carabas, you shall all be chopped into mincemeat!' When the King stopped his carriage and asked whose meadow it was, the terrified mowers answered in unison: 'It belongs to my Lord Marquis of Carabas!' The King was astounded by his guest's vast landholdings.

Puss ran ahead and threatened reapers cutting a golden wheat field, who likewise told the King that the harvest belonged to the Marquis of Carabas. At last, Puss arrived at a magnificent castle of stone and marble belonging to a ferocious, immensely wealthy ogre, who owned all the surrounding lands and could transform himself into any beast at will.

Puss knocked boldly and asked for an audience. Bowing low, Puss said: 'I have heard it reported, noble lord, that you possess the supernatural power to transform yourself into any beast—such as a lion or an elephant.'

'It is true!' roared the ogre, and in a flash, he changed into a terrifying lion with a thunderous roar. Puss was so frightened that he scrambled up the tapestries to the gutters, nearly slipping on his leather boots.

When the ogre resumed his human form, laughing heartily, Puss climbed down, panting. 'That was marvelous!' said the cat. 'Yet surely it is completely impossible for a lord of your mighty stature to change into a creature as tiny as a rat or a mouse?'

'Impossible?' sneered the vain ogre. 'Watch this!'

In an instant, the ogre shrank into a tiny brown mouse that scurried across the floor. Puss leaped like lightning, pounced upon the mouse, and swallowed him in a single gulp!

Hearing the rumbling of the royal coach crossing the drawbridge, Puss ran to the gate, bowed low, and proclaimed: 'Welcome, Your Majesty, to the chateau of my Lord Marquis of Carabas!'

The King was dazzled by the castle's grandeur. A lavish feast, which the ogre had prepared for his friends, was served in the banquet hall. Delighted by the young man's nobility, modesty, and vast wealth, the King declared: 'It depends only on yourself, Lord Marquis, whether you shall become my son-in-law.'

The miller's son accepted with heartfelt gratitude, and that very evening, he married the beautiful princess. As for Puss, he was made a great lord of the realm, and from that day forward, he never chased mice again, except as an amusing recreation.
moral: Ingenuity, tact, and enterprise are often worth more than an inherited fortune.

full_text:
Once upon a time, there lived a haughty widow who had two daughters. The elder sister resembled her mother in every feature and temperament: both were so proud, arrogant, and sour-tempered that no neighbor could live beside them in harmony. The younger daughter, on the other hand, was the true portrait of her deceased father—gentle, modest, kind-hearted, and endowed with beauty beyond compare.

Because humans often cherish those who reflect their own faults, the cruel mother doted blindly upon the elder daughter, pampering her with silks and sweets, while she harbored a bitter hatred for the younger. She made the gentle girl dress in threadbare rags, eat table scraps in the kitchen, and perform all the heavy domestic labor of the household.

Twice every day, the poor younger daughter was compelled to carry a massive earthenware pitcher more than half a league through the rocky woods to fetch sweet spring water from a secluded fountain.

One hot afternoon, as the weary maiden knelt by the crystal pool and filled her jar, an elderly, bent woman dressed in ragged homespun stepped from the forest and said in a trembling voice: 'Pray, my pretty child, give a drink of water to a poor old woman who is faint with thirst.'

'With all my heart, good mother,' the gentle girl answered with a radiant smile. She immediately rinsed the pitcher with fresh water, drew the coolest, purest water from the deep bubbling spring, and held the jar securely with her own hands so that the weary traveler might drink with comfort and ease.

When the old woman had quenched her thirst, her eyes shone with magical light. She was not a mortal beggar, but a great and benevolent fairy who had assumed the disguise of a poor peasant to test the maiden's virtue. 'You are so fair, so good, and so courteous,' said the fairy, 'that I must bestow a gift upon you. This is my blessing: for every word you utter, there shall fall from your mouth either a fragrant flower, a shining pearl, or a sparkling diamond.'

When the girl returned home, her mother scolded her harshly for tarrying so long at the fountain. 'I beg your pardon, mother, for being so slow,' the maiden said meekly.

As she spoke, there dropped from her sweet lips two crimson roses, two luminous pearls, and two brilliant diamonds of the first water!

'What is this I behold?' shrieked the astonished mother, greed sparkling in her eyes. 'Do I see pearls and diamonds falling from your mouth? How comes this to pass, my daughter?' (It was the very first time in the girl's life that her mother had called her daughter).

The honest girl recounted her encounter with the old woman at the fountain, and as she spoke, a shower of thirty diamonds, rubies, and fragrant lilies tumbled upon the table flagstones.

'Look at this!' the mother shouted to her elder daughter. 'See what fortune falls from your sister's tongue? You must go to the fountain immediately and receive the same boon! Take this large silver pitcher; fetch water, and when an old woman asks for a drink, speak to her with great honeyed words!'

'Indeed!' scoffed the spoiled elder sister. 'Must I soil my slippers and carry a heavy jar like a common servant girl? Let the kitchen wench go!'

'I command you to go!' shouted the furious mother.

Pouting and grumbling, the proud girl seized the finest silver flagon from the dining cupboard and stomped into the forest.

When she reached the bubbling spring, she saw emerging from the grove a magnificent lady dressed in shimmering cloth of gold and pearls, who approached and asked for a drink from her flagon. It was the same fairy, who had now assumed the appearance of a royal princess to discover whether the elder daughter's arrogance had any bounds.

'Did I come all this way through the briars to serve water to a fine court lady?' sneered the arrogant girl, tossing her head in disdain. 'Did I carry a silver flagon just to give you a drink? Quench your thirst from the spring with your own hands, or die of thirst for all I care!'

The fairy looked upon her without anger, but with stern majesty. 'Since you have so little courtesy and such a venomous heart,' said the fairy, 'receive my gift: for every word you speak, there shall drop from your mouth an ugly toad, an asp, or a crawling viper!'

The haughty girl hurried back to the house, eager to demand her reward. As she crossed the threshold, her mother embraced her eagerly: 'Well, my dearest child, did you meet the fairy?'

'Yes, mother!' the daughter snapped, opening her mouth to boast.

Instantly, two hideous, warted toads and two hissing green vipers leaped from her lips and slithered across the floor!

'Horror!' cried the mother, recoiling in terror. 'What evil magic is this? It must be the fault of your wretched sister! I shall beat her within an inch of her life!'

The mother rushed into the kitchen with a broom handle, but the terrified younger daughter slipped through the back door and fled deep into the wilderness.

Sitting upon a fallen mossy trunk in the forest, weeping bitter tears over her undeserved exile, the gentle maiden was found by the King's eldest son, who was returning from a stag hunt. Struck by her heavenly beauty and her solitary distress, the prince dismounted and asked why she wept in the wild woods.

'Alas, my lord,' she answered softly, 'my mother has driven me from our home.'

As she spoke, five luminous pearls and four brilliant diamonds fell from her lips onto her threadbare apron. Amazed by this divine marvel, the prince questioned her gently, and hearing the story of her kindness at the fountain, he realized that a maiden whose soul was so pure and whose words were literally jewels would make the finest queen in all Christendom. He lifted her onto his royal stallion, carried her to the capital, and married her in the royal cathedral amidst the rejoicing of the people.

As for the wicked elder sister, her temper grew so foul and her mouth dropped so many venomous serpents that her own mother grew terrified and drove her from the house. Despised by all who encountered her, the miserable girl wandered into the stony mountains and perished in obscurity, while virtue and kindness reigned in honor and love.
moral: Gentle courtesy and a willing heart bring blessings richer than jewels, while arrogance and pride bring shame and ruin.

full_text:
Once there lived a noble gentleman who took for his second wife the haughtiest and most overbearing woman that was ever seen. She had two daughters of her own who matched her in pride, spite, and selfish folly. The gentleman had a young daughter of incomparable sweetness and goodness of heart, inherited from her deceased mother, who had been the best woman in the world.

No sooner was the marriage concluded than the stepmother began to vent her bitter jealousy. She could not endure the young girl's gentle virtues, which made her own daughters appear disagreeable by comparison. She assigned the sweet girl the vilest domestic tasks: scouring the heavy copper cauldrons, scrubbing the marble staircases, and dusting the private bedchambers of the two sisters, where they slept in feather beds before full-length mirrors, while she herself slept in a dreary attic garret on a straw pallet.

When the poor girl finished her exhausting chores, she would sit by the chimney corner amidst the ashes and cinders to warm her shivering hands. Because of this, the household cruelly nicknamed her Cinder-slut, though the younger sister, who was slightly less malicious than the elder, called her Cendrillon, or Cinderella. Yet despite her worn, ash-stained smock, Cinderella was a hundred times more beautiful than her sisters dressed in their costliest silks.

It happened that the King's son gave a magnificent ball lasting two nights, inviting all the persons of distinction across the kingdom. The two proud sisters were beside themselves with excitement. They debated their attire endlessly: 'I shall wear my red velvet robe trimmed with English lace,' declared the elder. 'I,' said the younger, 'shall wear my gold-embroidered cloak and my necklace of five hundred diamonds.'

They summoned Cinderella to iron their linens, crimp their lace ruffles, and dress their hair, knowing she had exquisite taste. As she pinned their ribbons, they mocked her: 'Cinderella, would you not love to go to the royal ball?'

'Alas, sisters,' she replied gently, 'you only mock me; it is not for a cinder-girl to attend such splendor.'

When the sisters departed in their gilded carriage, Cinderella watched them go and burst into tears. Suddenly, her fairy godmother appeared before her in the hearth-light, carrying a slender wand of gold.

'What is the matter, my dear godchild?' the fairy asked softly.

'I wish... I wish I could...' Cinderella choked on her sobs.

'You wish you could go to the prince's ball, do you not?' smiled the godmother. 'Be a good girl, and I will see you go.'

'Run into the kitchen garden,' said the fairy, 'and fetch me the finest pumpkin you can find.' Cinderella ran and plucked the largest golden pumpkin, though she could not conceive how it could carry her to a dance. The fairy scooped out its seeds, tapped the rind with her wand, and instantly the pumpkin transformed into a magnificent royal coach lined with rose satin and gilded with burnished gold!

Looking into the mouse trap, the fairy found six lively mice. She opened the trap door, and as each mouse scampered out, a touch of her wand transformed it into a majestic, dapple-gray carriage horse. For a coachman, Cinderella fetched a fat rat from the whiskers trap, whom the fairy touched and changed into a jolly coachman with the finest mustache seen in France. Six lizards caught behind the watering pot became tall, powdered footmen who hopped up behind the carriage in gold-braided livery as if they had done nothing else their whole lives.

Then the fairy touched Cinderella's ragged apron. In a flash, her rags turned into a gown of cloth-of-gold and silver, sewn with seed pearls and diamonds. Onto her delicate feet, the fairy slipped a pair of slippers made of pure, sparkling glass—the prettiest in all creation.

'Go and enjoy yourself, my child,' the godmother warned, 'but mark well this command: you must not stay a single moment past the stroke of midnight. If you tarry but a second longer, your coach will become a pumpkin again, your horses mice, your footmen lizards, and your gown threadbare rags.'

Cinderella promised, kissed her godmother, and drove away in delight.

When she arrived at the palace, the King's son was informed that a great foreign princess had arrived whom no one knew. He ran to receive her, led her into the ballroom, and the music and dancing ceased in wonder. 'How beautiful she is!' whispered the courtiers, while the old King murmured to the Queen that he had not seen so lovely a creature in fifty years.

The prince danced with her all evening and could not take his eyes from her. Cinderella graciously sat beside her two sisters, sharing the candied oranges the prince had given her, but they failed to recognize their ash-covered drudge in this radiant royal guest. At a quarter to twelve, Cinderella curtsied to the King and Queen and hastened home, arriving in time to thank her godmother.

The second night, the ball was even more splendid. Cinderella arrived in an attire that surpassed the first in magnificence. The prince was constantly at her side, whispering courtly compliments, and Cinderella was so entranced by his devotion that she forgot her godmother's warning.

Suddenly, the great palace clock began to strike midnight: Dong! Dong!

Cinderella started up in horror and fled like a deer down the grand marble stairway. The prince leaped up and pursued her, but she was too swift. Yet in her frantic haste, one of her sparkling glass slippers slipped from her left foot, and she had no time to recover it.

She reached her home out of breath, on foot, dressed in her old rags, having nothing left of her magnificence except one tiny glass slipper that matched the one she had lost.

The prince found the exquisite slipper on the stair, picked it up with tender care, and gazed at it with longing. A few days later, royal trumpets sounded throughout the city: the King's son proclaimed that he would marry the maiden whose foot precisely fit the little glass slipper.

Gentlemen of the chamber carried the slipper to princesses, duchesses, and all the ladies of the court, but in vain. At last, it was brought to the home of Cinderella's stepmother. The two sisters strained, pulled, and squeezed their feet, but they could not push even their toes inside.

Watching from the corner, Cinderella smiled and said softly: 'Let me see if it will fit my foot.'

Her sisters burst into scornful laughter: 'What! Must this kitchen drudge try the prince's slipper?'

The royal officer looked at Cinderella, noting the delicate grace of her countenance, and said: 'My orders are strict; every maiden in the realm must try the slipper.'

He knelt before Cinderella, holding out the crystal shoe. Her slender foot slipped into the slipper effortlessly, fitting like molten wax. While her sisters stared in dumbfounded shock, Cinderella reached into her apron pocket and drew forth the second glass slipper, placing it upon her right foot!

At that instant, the fairy godmother appeared, touched Cinderella's rags, and transformed them into a bridal gown of starlight. The two sisters recognized the great princess of the ball and fell at her feet, weeping and begging forgiveness for their long cruelty.

Cinderella lifted them up, embraced them with tears of genuine affection, and said she forgave them with all her heart, asking only that they love her always. She was conducted to the royal palace in triumph, and married the prince with immense joy. Having room in her heart for only generosity, Cinderella gave her two sisters noble apartments in the palace and married them that very day to two honorable lords of the court.
moral: Grace and kindness of heart are greater than beauty, and forgiveness is the finest ornament of nobility.

full_text:
Once upon a time, a queen gave birth to a prince who was so misshapen and ugly that it was feared for a time he was scarcely human. He had a crooked spine, awkward limbs, and a comical tuft of bright red hair sprouting upon his crown. Yet as the queen wept over her newborn, a wise fairy who attended the birth comforted her, saying: 'Grieve not, Your Majesty. Your son shall possess so brilliant, charming, and profound a mind that no one shall notice his physical flaws. Moreover, I bestow upon him this supernatural gift: he shall have the power to impart the same measure of wit, eloquence, and intelligence to the person he loves most in all the world.'

Because of the comical red crest upon his head, the boy was named Riquet with the Tuft, or Ricky of the Tuft. As he grew, his words were so witty, his manners so courteous, and his wisdom so luminous that the greatest scholars and philosophers of the continent traveled to converse with him, enchanted by his companionship.

In a neighboring realm, another queen gave birth to twin daughters. The first was so astonishingly beautiful that the mother rejoiced, but the fairy present warned: 'She shall be radiant as the dawn, but she shall be equally dull-witted and lacking in sense.' The second twin was born remarkably plain, but the fairy granted her the gift of exquisite wit and charm.

As the years passed, the prophecies came to pass. Wherever the twin princesses went, people flocked at first to admire the dazzling beauty of the elder sister. But the moment she opened her mouth, her foolish remarks, awkward silences, and silly giggles drove everyone away to gather around the plainer younger sister, whose sparkling wit and delightful stories held the court spellbound. The beautiful elder princess wept bitter tears of humiliation, wishing with all her soul that she possessed half the intelligence of her plain sister, even at the cost of all her beauty.

One morning, having fled the palace to hide her shame, the beautiful princess was walking in a secluded forest when she encountered a short, misshapen gentleman dressed in magnificent courtly robes, wearing a distinctive tuft of red hair. It was Prince Ricky of the Tuft, who had fallen in love with portraits of her beauty and had traveled to her father's kingdom.

Seeing her weeping, Ricky bowed with courtly grace: 'Madam, how can a lady endowed with such heavenly beauty abandon herself to sorrow?'

'Alas, sir,' she replied heavily, 'I am as stupid as I am fair, and I would rather be the ugliest creature on earth if only I had wit and good sense.'

'Madam,' smiled Ricky, 'wit is not a gift that lies beyond your reach. I possess the fairy power to grant the highest intelligence to the lady I choose for my bride. If you will promise to marry me on this exact day one year hence, I will make you the wittiest and most charming woman in the world.'

Believing that a year was an eternity and that she might easily find a way out of the promise later, the foolish princess eagerly agreed. The moment she spoke her assent, a wonderful illumination flooded her mind. New thoughts, brilliant metaphors, and crystal logic blossomed in her understanding. She conversed with Ricky with such elegance, humor, and depth that she could hardly recognize herself.

Returning to the royal palace, the transformed princess stunned the entire court. Her father, the King, began consulting her on intricate treaties and statecraft; foreign ambassadors marveled at her diplomatic brilliance, and princes from every empire arrived to seek her hand in marriage.

A full year slipped away like a golden dream. Walking in the forest to ponder which of her noble suitors she should accept, she heard a strange rumbling beneath the earth. Kneeling by the grass, she saw the ground open to reveal an underground kitchen where hundreds of dwarf cooks were preparing an enormous wedding feast with spits of roasted partridges and cakes of sugar.

'For whom are you preparing this grand banquet?' the princess asked in surprise.

'For our master, Prince Ricky of the Tuft,' the head chef replied, 'whose wedding is to be celebrated tomorrow!'

The princess gasped; the year was up, and she had completely forgotten her promise! At that moment, Prince Ricky stepped from the trees, bowing low with love and devotion. 'I have come, fair princess, to claim the hand you promised me.'

The princess hesitated, troubled by her newfound intellect. 'Prince Ricky,' she said, 'when I made that promise, I was a foolish girl who understood nothing. Now that you have given me reason, how can you expect a wise princess to wed a prince who is so misshapen?'

Ricky smiled with gentle dignity: 'If I were a cruel, wicked, or foolish prince, you would have every right to refuse me. But is there anything in my soul, my character, or my devotion that displeases you?'

'No,' she confessed honestly, 'your character is the noblest I have ever met.'

'Then what stands between us except my outer appearance?' asked the prince. 'Did you know that the same fairy who gave me the power to make you clever also gave you the power to make the man you love handsome?'

'Is it true?' cried the princess. 'With all my heart, I wish that you may become the most handsome, noble, and well-proportioned prince in all the world!'

No sooner had she uttered the wish than the spell of love and magic worked its miracle. To the princess's eyes, Ricky's crooked spine straightened into a tall, athletic stature; his awkward gait became the majestic stride of a warrior; his comical tuft of red hair became waves of rich auburn locks, and his countenance shone with manly beauty and gentleness. (Some chroniclers whisper that the fairy magic did not change his limbs at all, but that the princess, having learned to love his noble soul, saw only beauty in the face of her beloved).

Together, they returned to the palace with joy. The King gladly gave his consent, and Ricky of the Tuft and his witty princess were wed in splendor, proving that love creates its own beauty, and that true affection sees through the eyes of the heart.
moral: True beauty is not merely skin deep; love and understanding transform the qualities of the soul into grace.

full_text:
Once upon a time, a poor woodcutter and his wife lived in a humble thatched hut in the heart of a great, shadowy forest. They had seven sons, born in rapid succession: the eldest was ten years old and the youngest was only seven. The youngest boy was remarkably small; when he was born, he was scarcely larger than a man's thumb, wherefore he was named Little Thumbling, or Hop-o'-My-Thumb.

Though he was the smallest and spoke very little, Thumbling was the sharpest and most observant child in the province. While his elder brothers babbled, he listened carefully, storing every word in his quick mind. His parents, however, foolishly mistook his silence for dullness and often laid upon him the blame for every misfortune.

A terrible famine swept over the land. Grain prices rose so high that the poor woodcutter could no longer earn enough to buy a crust of bread for his starving boys. One evening, sitting by the dying embers while the children were asleep in their trundle beds, the woodcutter wept: 'Wife, my heart breaks to see our boys waste away before our eyes. Tomorrow morning, we must lead them into the deepest thicket of the forest to gather faggots, and while they are busy binding sticks, we will slip away and leave them. It is better that they be found by some rich hunter than that we watch them starve in our arms.'

The mother wept bitterly, but extreme misery overcame her reluctance.

Hop-o'-My-Thumb, who was lying awake under his father's stool, heard every word. Instead of crying, he crept out of the hut at dawn, ran to the bed of a nearby stream, and filled his pockets with smooth, white flint pebbles.

After breakfast, the parents led the seven boys into the densest, darkest part of the wilderness. As they walked, Thumbling dropped the white pebbles one by one along the trail. When the woodcutter began chopping trees and the brothers were gathering brushwood, the parents stole away through a ravine.

Finding themselves alone in the gathering gloom, the six elder brothers wept aloud in terror. But Thumbling laughed: 'Fear not, brothers! Father and mother have left us, but follow me, and I will lead you safely home.' Guided by the white pebbles gleaming in the moonlight, Thumbling led his brothers straight back to their cottage.

Listening at the door, they heard their mother weeping: for that afternoon, the lord of the manor had paid the woodcutter ten silver crowns for old debts, and the mother had purchased a great pot of beef, lamenting that her boys were not there to eat it. Thumbling pushed open the door and shouted cheerfully: 'Here we are, mother!' Overjoyed, the parents fed them a bountiful supper.

When the silver was spent, hunger returned, and the parents resolved to abandon the boys again, leading them even deeper into the woods. Hop-o'-My-Thumb intended to gather more pebbles, but his mother had locked the cottage door. Instead, he crumbled his morning crust of bread in his pocket, dropping crumbs along the trail as they walked.

When the parents deserted them, Thumbling sought his breadcrumbs, but in vain: a flock of woodland sparrows and thrushes had pecked up every single crumb! The seven boys were hopelessly lost in the black forest, surrounded by howling wolves.

Climbing to the top of a tall pine, Thumbling spotted a flicker of candlelight beyond the forest canopy. Gathering his brothers, he led them toward the light until they arrived at a massive stone mansion with iron bars on the windows.

A kind-hearted woman answered their knock. 'Alas, poor children!' she cried. 'Do you not know where you are? This is the castle of a monstrous ogre who feasts upon the flesh of little children!'

'Madam,' Thumbling pleaded with tears, 'if you do not hide us, the wolves will devour us tonight. We would rather be eaten by the master of the house if it must be, but perhaps your compassion may soften his heart.'

Moved to pity, the ogress hid the boys under a bed. Soon, a thunderous stamping shook the floorboards: the ogre entered, smelling fresh meat. Poking around the room with his iron-tipped club, he pulled the seven trembling boys from beneath the bed.

'Aha, wife!' roared the ogre, licking his lips. 'Here is a delicate roast for tomorrow's feast with my friends!'

The clever wife persuaded him to spare them until morning, as they had already eaten a fat sheep. The ogre ordered them put to bed in the chamber of his seven little daughters, who slept in a row wearing golden crowns upon their heads.

Thumbling noticed that the ogre was fond of tasting his food at midnight when he was in his cups. Taking the golden crowns from the sleeping daughters, he placed them on his brothers' heads and his own, and put their coarse wool nightcaps upon the ogre's daughters.

Sure enough, at midnight, the ogre stumbled into the dark bedchamber with his carving knife. Feeling the wool caps, he muttered: 'Aha! Here are the little rascals!' and in his drunken stupor, he dealt with his own daughters before stumbling back to bed.

The moment the ogre's snores shook the castle walls, Thumbling woke his brothers and they slipped through the garden wall into the forest.

At dawn, discovering his terrible error, the ogre roared with fury: 'Bring me my Seven-League Boots!' Putting on the magical boots, which expanded or contracted to fit any foot and allowed the wearer to cross seven leagues at a single stride, the ogre chased the boys like a hurricane.

Thumbling saw the giant bounding over mountains. He pushed his brothers into a hollow limestone cave beneath a high rock. Exhausted by his pursuit, the ogre lay down upon that very rock to rest and fell into a thunderous sleep.

Thumbling crept out, gently slipped the Seven-League Boots from the ogre's feet, and pulled them onto his own paws. The magical boots shrank to fit his little feet perfectly!

Leaving his brothers safely hidden, Thumbling sprinted in his magical boots straight to the ogre's castle. 'Madam,' he said to the weeping ogress, 'your husband has been captured by mountain bandits who swear to kill him unless you send all his gold and jewels! He commanded me to wear his Seven-League Boots as a token that you should deliver the ransom to me without delay!'

Terrified for her husband's life, the woman loaded Thumbling with sacks of emeralds, diamonds, and gold. Thumbling ran back, collected his six brothers, and led them home in triumph to their astonished parents.

With their boundless treasure, the family lived in great comfort and honor. Thumbling later served as the King's chief courier, using his Seven-League Boots to carry urgent dispatches across the realm, earning the love of the sovereign and the eternal gratitude of his brothers, proving forever that size is nothing compared to courage and wit.
moral: The smallest and least esteemed child often possesses the sharpest mind and becomes the salvation of the entire family.

title: Griselidis - Griselda (verse tale)
summary: In the ancient and fertile province of Saluzzo, there ruled a young and handsome prince named Walter, who spent his youth in the pleasure...
full_text:
In the ancient and fertile province of Saluzzo, there ruled a young and handsome prince named Walter, who spent his youth in the pleasures of the hunt, neglecting all thoughts of marriage. Anxious for the peace of the realm, his loyal subjects gathered before his palace gates, petitioning him with humble prayers to choose a noble bride so that the kingdom might never fall into disputed succession.

Moved by their devotion, the prince agreed, but declared that he alone would choose his wife, regardless of birth or dowry.

Nearby, in a tiny hamlet of thatched huts, dwelt an honest, impoverished shepherd named Giannucole, whose daughter Griselda was the marvel of the valley. Though she wore coarse homespun and tended her father's meager flock of sheep upon the stony hills, her heart was a sanctuary of filial piety, modesty, and gentle grace. She rose before dawn to milk the ewes, spun wool by the hearth, and tended her aged father with tenderest devotion.

The prince had often observed her from afar during his hunts, noting how her pure spirit shone through her humble station.

On the appointed wedding day, grand lords and ladies assembled at the prince's palace, wondering who the noble bride would be. To their astonishment, Walter rode out to the shepherd's humble hut. Entering the low doorway, the prince addressed the blushing maiden before her father: 'Griselda, I desire to make you my princess and my wife. But you must promise me this solemn vow: that whatever trials or commands I may lay upon you, you will submit to my will with a patient heart, without murmur, frown, or sorrow.'

Griselda bowed her head in meek reverence: 'My lord and sovereign, I am unworthy of this honor. I vow that neither in word, nor deed, nor thought shall I ever oppose your royal will.'

The court ladies stripped off her coarse shepherdess rags and clothed her in robes of gold brocade, placing an emerald coronet upon her braided hair. The wedding was celebrated with music and joy, and Griselda carried herself with such natural majesty, wisdom, and sweetness that all the people adored her as if she had been born of royal blood.

Soon, she bore a beautiful daughter. Yet a dark and cruel obsession took root in the prince's mind: he resolved to test his wife's fidelity and patience to the utmost extremity.

He sent a stern officer to her chamber to seize the infant daughter, leading Griselda to believe the child was to be put to death because the nobles despised an heir of peasant blood. With tears coursing down her cheeks, Griselda gently kissed her baby, made the sign of blessing upon its forehead, and surrendered the child without a single word of anger or rebellion. (Unknown to her, the prince secretly sent the infant to be raised in luxury at a distant court).

Years later, Griselda bore a fine son. Again the prince subjected her to the same bitter ordeal, taking the boy away under the pretext of state necessity. Griselda bore the anguish with unbroken serenity, saying only: 'My lord, I and my children belong wholly to you; do with us as pleases your judgment.'

Finally, after twelve years, the prince forged letters from Rome claiming that the Pope had granted him a divorce so that he might take a high-born bride. He summoned Griselda before the entire court, commanded her to surrender her jewels and royal robes, and ordered her to return barefoot to her father's cottage.

Griselda removed her crown, handed back her rings, and said with quiet dignity: 'My lord, naked did I leave my father's threshold, and naked must I return. I thank you for the honor of having been your wife, and I pray that heaven may grant you happiness with your new bride.' Dressed only in a plain white shift, she walked back to her father's hut, cheered by the weeping populace who revered her saintly patience.

A few weeks later, the prince summoned her back to the palace—not as a guest, but to sweep the flagstones and prepare the banquet chambers for his incoming bride. Griselda labored with willing humility, ensuring every hall was adorned with garlands.

When the wedding guests arrived, accompanied by a radiant twelve-year-old maiden and an eight-year-old boy, Griselda welcomed them with gentle courtesy, praising the young girl's beauty.

Overcome by her sublime, unwavering love, Prince Walter could endure the trial no longer. Tears streamed down his cheeks as he caught Griselda in his arms before the assembled court: 'It is enough, my beloved Griselda! You have triumphed over every test of human patience! You alone are my wife, and these two children are none other than our own beloved daughter and son, preserved and raised in honor!'

The court erupted in tears of joy and thunderous applause. Griselda embraced her children with cries of ecstasy, dressed once more in royal purple. Prince Walter repented of his cruel experiments, and for the rest of their long lives, Griselda reigned with wisdom, love, and honored renown, an immortal exemplar of patient virtue and constant love.
moral: Patient virtue and steadfast fidelity endure through every trial, overcoming cruelty and earning enduring honor.

title: Peau d'Ane - Donkey Skin
summary: Once upon a time, there reigned a great and wealthy king whose stables housed the most extraordinary marvel in all the world: a marvelous...
full_text:
Once upon a time, there reigned a great and wealthy king whose stables housed the most extraordinary marvel in all the world: a marvelous donkey whose stall, instead of common straw and filth, was carpeted with velvet, for every morning, the beast dropped upon the flagstones pure gold coins, Spanish doubloons, and Portuguese crusados, supplying the kingdom with inexhaustible wealth.

The king lived in bliss with his beautiful queen, who bore him a daughter endowed with heavenly grace. But a sudden sickness struck the queen. On her deathbed, fearful that her grieving husband might fall prey to a cruel second wife, she made him swear a solemn oath: that he would never remarry unless he found a maiden whose beauty, virtue, and wisdom surpassed her own.

After years of mourning, the king sought a new queen, but none in the world matched the late queen's perfection—except his own grown daughter. Confused by grief and ill-counsel, the king conceived the unlawful desire to marry the princess.

Horrified by this unnatural suit, the virtuous princess fled to the secluded grotto of her fairy godmother, the Lilac Fairy. 'Fear not, my child,' the wise fairy advised. 'Do not oppose your father with harsh words, for that would provoke his wrath. Instead, demand impossible conditions. Ask him first for a dress the color of the clear weather and blue skies; until he provides it, you will not listen to his proposal.'

The king summoned his master tailors, threatening them with the gallows unless they succeeded. Working night and day, they created a gown woven of azure silk so luminous that it mirrored the purest summer morning.

The princess returned to the fairy in despair. 'Demand next a gown the color of the silver moon,' the Lilac Fairy instructed. The king's embroiderers worked by moonlight and brought a robe of woven silver that shone with heavenly radiance.

'Demand now a gown the color of the sun,' said the fairy. The king melted gold ingots into threads finer than gossamer and encrusted the fabric with diamonds, producing a dress so dazzling that mortals could scarcely look upon it without shielding their eyes.

Trembling, the princess returned to the grotto: 'What shall I do now, godmother? He has granted every wish!'

'Now,' smiled the fairy, 'demand the skin of his marvelous gold-bearing donkey. He will never consent to sacrifice the source of all his wealth.'

Yet the king's obsession was so blind that without hesitation, he ordered the donkey slaughtered and had its coarse, shaggy hide presented to his daughter.

'Now you must flee,' the Lilac Fairy commanded. She touched the princess's magnificent dresses, which shrank into a small walnut shell that could be hidden in a pocket. 'Smear your face with soot, wrap yourself in this foul donkey's skin, and run into the wilderness. No one will recognize you. Whenever you tap this ebony wand, your walnut shell and dresses will appear.'

The princess slipped from the palace under the cover of night. Wrapped in the crude hide, she wandered through distant provinces, begging for employment. Because she looked so wretched, villagers threw stones at her, calling her 'Donkeyskin.'

At last, she found employment as a scullery maid on a vast royal estate, cleaning the turkey coops, scrubbing the grease from iron kettles, and sleeping in a damp hovel behind the pigsties. Yet through all her degradation, her gentle heart remained pure and patient.

On Sundays, having finished her dirty labor, Donkeyskin would wash the grime from her face, lock her wooden door, and open her walnut shell. Dressing in her gown of clear skies, the silver moon, or the golden sun, she would admire her reflection and sing like an angel, finding solace in her secret grace.

One afternoon, the king's handsome son, who was hunting in the forest, wandered into the courtyard and peeked through the keyhole of the solitary hovel. He gasped in wonder: instead of the filthy scullery maid, he beheld a maiden of celestial beauty, dressed in a robe of sunbeams and diamonds!

Overcome with love, the prince returned to the palace and fell into a burning fever of longing. The royal physicians were helpless. When his weeping mother begged him to reveal his desire, he whispered: 'I desire a cake baked by the hands of Donkeyskin, and nothing else can heal me.'

Though disgusted by the idea of food prepared by the filthy drudge, the queen ordered Donkeyskin to bake a cake. The princess washed her hands in rosewater, sifted fine flour, added fresh cream and eggs, and kneaded the dough. As she worked, a tiny emerald ring of exquisite workmanship slipped from her finger and became concealed within the cake.

When the cake was baked to golden perfection, the prince devoured it eagerly. Biting into the crumb, his teeth struck the emerald ring. He concealed the jewel under his pillow and grew more passionately in love than ever.

The prince declared he would marry only the maiden whose finger fit the tiny ring. Trumpets sounded, and ladies of the court, noblewomen, and peasant girls flocked to the castle, but the ring was so slender that none could slip it past their knuckle.

'Have all the women in the realm tried the ring?' the prince demanded.

'All,' answered the chamberlain, 'except filthy Donkeyskin who cleans the turkey coops.'

'Bring her here!' ordered the prince.

The court laughed scornfully as the wretched figure in the foul donkey skin entered the marble hall. But when the prince held out the emerald ring, her slender, delicate finger slid into it effortlessly!

At that moment, the princess let the coarse donkey skin fall to the floor. The Lilac Fairy appeared, touching her with her wand, and revealed the princess clothed in her magnificent gown of sunbeams and diamonds, radiant as the dawn!

The king and queen embraced her with tears of admiration, and preparations were made for a royal wedding. Among the invited monarchs was the princess's father, whose mind had been cured of his madness by the fairy's counsel. Weeping tears of joy, he asked his daughter's forgiveness and bestowed upon her his entire kingdom, proving that true virtue may be eclipsed by sorrow, but like the morning sun, it rises in glorious triumph.
moral: True modesty and virtue may be concealed beneath the humblest disguise, but like pure gold, their radiance cannot be hidden.

title: Les Souhaits ridicules - The Ridiculous Wishes
summary: Once upon a time, a poor woodcutter lived in a humble forest cottage, spending his days in backbreaking toil, cutting timber from dawn to...
keywords: les souhaits ridicules - the ridiculous wishes
full_text:
Once upon a time, a poor woodcutter lived in a humble forest cottage, spending his days in backbreaking toil, cutting timber from dawn to dusk for a few copper pennies. Weary of his perpetual poverty, he sat upon a fallen oak one evening and loudly complained to the heavens: 'How cruel is my fate! I labor like a beast of burden, yet I never have enough bread to satisfy my hunger, nor a good coat to keep out the winter frost. Why was I born to suffer, while lazy lords feast in silk and luxury?'

As he uttered these bitter lamentations, a blinding flash of light illuminated the forest clearing, accompanied by a pleasant fragrance of cedar and frankincense. Standing before him was the benevolent woodland spirit, crowned with oak leaves and holding a staff of silver.

'Cease your weeping, honest woodsman,' the spirit said in a voice like rustling leaves. 'The guardians of the forest have heard your complaints. I grant you this supernatural favor: the next three wishes you formulate in your mind and speak with your lips shall be granted to you, whatever they may be. But ponder your desires with wisdom, for upon your choice depends your eternal happiness.'

With these words, the spirit dissolved into the evening mist.

Wild with excitement, the woodcutter threw down his axe and sprinted home like a young boy. Bursting into his kitchen, he embraced his wife and shouted: 'Rejoice, wife! Our poverty is ended forever! The great spirit has granted me three wishes! We shall have mountains of gold, palaces of marble, and empires of land! But first, let us celebrate. Stoke the fire and pour a jug of your best country cider!'

The prudent wife brought a pitcher of cider and glasses, but cautioned him: 'Husband, when fortune smiles so suddenly, we must act with the greatest prudence. Let us eat our supper and wait until tomorrow morning to formulate our three wishes, when our minds are calm and free from excitement.'

'You speak wisely, wife,' agreed the woodcutter. 'Patience is indeed the mother of good counsel.'

Sitting by the warm fireplace, sipping his sweet cider, the woodcutter noticed the fragrant smoke of the oak logs and felt a pleasant hunger stirring in his stomach. Forgetting all his resolutions, he sighed contentedly and said without thinking: 'Ah! What a fine fire! How delightful it would be if we had a long, juicy black sausage to roast over these glowing coals!'

No sooner had the words left his lips than a loud swoosh echoed in the chimney. Down tumbled a magnificent, plump, savory black sausage, winding itself upon the hot hearthstones like a serpent!

The wife stared in disbelief, then turned upon her husband with blazing eyes: 'You miserable, brainless fool! You had the choice of an empire, golden crowns, diamonds, and dukedoms, and you squandered our very first wish upon a piece of meat? A sausage! May the plague take you and your greedy belly!'

The woodcutter hung his head in shame, stammering apologies, but his wife's sharp tongue knew no mercy. For an entire hour, she paced the kitchen floor, heaping insults upon his head, calling him an idiot, a ruined wretch, and the disgrace of Christendom.

At last, losing all patience and stung to the quick by her relentless scolding, the woodcutter banged his fist on the table and roared in blind fury: 'A curse upon your shrewish tongue! I wish that wretched sausage were stuck fast to the tip of your miserable nose!'

Instantly, the magical sausage sprang from the hearth like a coiled spring, flew through the air, and glued itself securely to the very tip of the wife's nose!

The woman gasped, reached up, and shrieked in horror. She pulled with both hands, but the sausage was as firmly attached as if it were part of her flesh. It dangled down past her chin like an absurd elephant's trunk, twitching with every word she spoke.

The woodcutter looked upon her with a mixture of terror and remorse. Only one wish remained!

The wife wept through her sausage: 'What good is all the gold in the world, what good are marble palaces and queens' robes to me, if I must walk among mortals with a long black sausage hanging from my face? Every child in the city will point and laugh!'

The woodcutter pondered deeply. With his final wish, he could still make himself a mighty king of infinite riches, but his beloved wife would be a laughingstock for the rest of her days. He remembered their years of shared hardship, her loyalty, and their simple love.

Turning to her with tenderness, he said: 'Dear wife, gold cannot buy peace, and vanity brings only misery.'

Facing the ceiling, the woodcutter spoke his third and final wish: 'I wish that the sausage would detach from my wife's nose and fall harmlessly to the hearth!'

In an instant, the sausage dropped to the flagstones with a soft thud, leaving the wife's nose as smooth and fair as it had ever been.

Embracing with tears of relief and humble joy, the woodcutter and his wife realized how close they had come to ruin through greed and anger. They picked up the savory sausage, roasted it over the coals, and ate it together with crusty bread and sweet cider—the most delicious meal of their lives. From that day forward, they worked with cheerful hearts, living in peace and contentment, rich in the wisdom that true happiness lies not in excessive wishes, but in enjoying what one has with love.
moral: Fools squander great opportunities on trivial whims; contentment, patience, and love are the truest riches.
